subtitle: What this has all been for
words.intro: You now have a German that can do what you ask of it. You can reach a judge, a mayor or a neighbour. You can read the small print and leave things unsaid. There’s only one thing still to learn. It’s a very short word, and in this last chapter somebody finally uses it.

grammar[0].subheading: From Guten Tag to the last word
grammar[0].blocks[0].note: If you really can’t tell, avoid the pronoun. Germans do this all the time: it’s an art.
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: Wie man es anbietet
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: The older person offers, or the senior, or, in the old rules, the woman. Say yes. Saying no is possible, but it will be remembered, possibly in a notebook.
grammar[0].fact: Calling a police officer *du* can really cost you money in Germany, though *Sie* can be used as an insult too. Courts have heard such cases. Once you’ve agreed to *du* you can’t go back, without something having gone badly wrong. So it isn’t a small word.
grammar[0].check.title: Mini-Check
grammar[1].subheading: The last table, and the last rule
grammar[1].blocks[0].title: From this book
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: It’s all yours. Now forget where it came from.
grammar[1].blocks[1].text: Everything in twelve books was so that you could choose. In the end, the sentence that matters may be very short: *Wird noch*. Your German is good enough now to write it about someone else.
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: Read a novel. Argue with a neighbour. Write something. Find someone in the first week of their German, who thinks *Guten Tag* is a sentence. Say something kind, and slowly. It’s your turn at the window.
grammar[1].fact: There’s no C3. From here on you’re simply someone who speaks German, with an accent you may keep. You got here on your own. Very few do. Glückwunsch, and Glück auf.

listen.intro: The last listening of the course. It has everything in it. Listen to it once, without stopping, and notice how much you no longer have to think about.
speak.intro: Analyse something you care about with the tutor. Then say what you’d tell someone in their first week of German.

document.intro: The last real document in these books. It’s a certificate from 1958, for Frau Ully Spier, born in 1910 in Luckenwalde, near Berlin. Her address is given as *Ramoth Hashavim, Israel*. Read that line, and read the two dates. Nobody says what happened in between.
document.fact: Germans who lost their citizenship under the Nazis, and their descendants, have a right to it back, under the Basic Law. It’s Article 116. This one sentence, *hat … die deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit erworben*, is all that the form could manage. You’ve learned to read what isn’t said.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Write what the page doesn’t say, in one short sentence.
reading.intro: Max took the test at last. He got 33 out of 33. Today, at the town hall, the certificates are being handed out to him and to 41 others. Maya’s come straight from a reading. Everyone is here in their best coats. The real reason for this page is what happens afterwards, on the stairs at Hofstraße 12.
reading.photos[0].caption: Ein Hinterhof, am Abend: Niemand schaut. Angeblich.
reading.photos[1].caption: Die Treppe: Hier kam sie herauf, mit einer Tasche.
reading.fact: First name with *Sie* has a name of its own: the *Hamburger Sie*. It’s rare, and it’s very warm, and very formal, and you’ll seldom be offered it. An older person usually makes the offer of *du*. Germans remember the day it happened, and some never get there at all.
